extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics, and readers interested in biography, compilation, and English oratory (general literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for composing and evaluating biographies, compilations, and spoken rhetoric (use of gesture)—what makes a life- narrative useful or truthful and when action aids speech. Focuses on truth, applicability, originality, and appropriateness of gesture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical value of biography
rubrics_metrics.description: "Biography is, of the various kinds of narrative writing, that which is most eagerly read, and most easily applied to the purposes of life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographies should aim to be readily applicable to readers' lives: prefer accounts that teach how people were made happy or how they erred in ordinary life rather than merely narrating spectacular or improbable events. Emphasize instructive, real incidents over extravagant invention; biographies are valuable because they lend practical lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veracity matters for adult curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: “In romances, when the wide field of possibility lies open to invention, ... the most artful tale raises little curiosity when it is known to be false.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adult readers lose interest in narratives they know to be false; fiction may still be valued for style or as pleasing diversion, but for instruction and lasting interest, verisimilitude or truth is essential. Use fiction for style/model or harmless amusement, not as a substitute for instructive truth when the audience expects reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autobiography's advantage: first-hand knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: “The writer of his own life has, at least, the first qualification of an historian, the knowledge of the truth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-person life-writing is privileged because the author has intimate access to facts and motives; this certainty reduces error and fortifies veracity. Still note the remaining danger of self-love—self-written lives can be truthful but require vigilance against self-justifying bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty of knowledge fortifies veracity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Certainty of knowledge not only excludes mistake, but fortifies veracity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer assertions grounded in direct knowledge rather than conjecture; what is fully known resists falsification and moral temptation. When possible, base narrative claims on known facts to increase credibility and ethical honesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware biographer bias (panegyric or censure)
rubrics_metrics.description: “He that writes the life of another is either his friend or his enemy, and wishes either to exalt his praise or aggravate his infamy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically evaluate motives: biographers are prone to partiality (panegyric) or maligning; expect distortions arising from gratitude, patriotism, party fidelity, or hatred. Readers and editors should demand evidence and impartiality; writers should disclose connections and resist partisan exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer ordinary, instructive incidents over heroic distance
rubrics_metrics.description: “The mischievous consequences of vice and folly...are best discovered by those relations which are levelled with the general surface of life...tell not how any man became great, but how he was made happy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the common, domestic, and moral facets of life that make lessons transferable to readers: avoid hiding the man beneath heroic decoration. Focus on familiar sensations and consequences to make characters instructive and relatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for compilations: add genuine value
rubrics_metrics.description: “That all compilations are useless, I do not assert...He that collects those under proper heads is very laudably employed...But the collections poured lately from the press have been seldom made at any great expense of time or inquiry...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compilations should not be lazy reworkings or plagiarism. Good compilations gather scattered, valuable fragments, organize them usefully, and facilitate readers' access to original insights. Compilers must inform themselves, examine originals, and contribute editorial judgment; avoid mere repetition or low-effort aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose-based assessment of writers (teach, please, amuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: “He that teaches us any thing which we knew not before, is undoubtedly to be reverenced as a master. He that conveys knowledge by more pleasing ways, may very properly be loved as a benefactor; and he that supplies life with innocent amusement, will be certainly caressed as a pleasing companion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a work by whether it fulfills its stated or evident purpose: originality and instruction (teaching new things) command reverence; elegance and pleasurable conveyance command affection; harmless amusement is also valuable. Evaluate form and content against intended function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and restraint: avoid needless repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: “To exact of every man who writes, that he should say something new, would be to reduce authors to a small number...Yet, surely, there ought to be some bounds to repetition; libraries ought no more to be heaped for ever with the same thoughts differently expressed...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While radical novelty cannot be demanded of every writer, editors and authors should avoid producing redundant works that merely restate known ideas without value. Strive for sufficient novelty or clear utility; refrain from multiplying near-duplicates that clutter literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of gesture in spoken rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is a complaint...that English oratory...is deficient and inefficacious, because our speakers want the grace and energy of action...If by sleight of hand, or nimbleness of foot, all these wonders can be performed, he that shall neglect to attain the free use of his limbs may be justly censured as criminally lazy. But...I have been hitherto inclined to doubt whether my countrymen are not blamed too hastily for their calm and motionless utterance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical action in speech only where it genuinely aids persuasion or comprehension. Excessive, labored gesticulation tends to be ridiculous and may not increase persuasive power among audiences committed to truth. Assess the audience and occasion—courts, parliaments, and judges value reasoned argument over theatrical gesture; don’t substitute motion for substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gestures as natural illustration or customary allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the pulpit little action can be proper, for action can illustrate nothing but that to which it may be referred by nature or by custom...He that imitates by his hand a motion which he describes, explains it by natural similitude; he that lays his hand on his breast, when he expresses pity, enforces his words by a customary allusion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing action, ensure it directly illustrates the spoken idea (natural similitude) or relies on established customary meaning (allusion). Appropriate, restrained gestures can clarify imagery or emphasize feeling for audiences who need sensory reinforcement; avoid arbitrary or novel contortions that distract.
